title: A scheme receiving a surjective universally closed morphism from an affine scheme is affine
statement: Let $f:X\to S$ be a morphism of schemes [def-pc-scheme]. Assume that $X$ is an affine scheme [def-pc-scheme], that $f$ is surjective, i.e. the map of underlying topological spaces $|X|\to|S|$ is surjective [def-weil-surjective-morphism], and that $f$ is universally closed, i.e. for every morphism $S'\to S$ the base change $X\times_SS'\to S'$ is a closed map of underlying topological spaces [def-weil-proper-morphism]. Then $S$ is an affine scheme. (In particular this holds when $f$ is surjective and integral, an integral morphism being universally closed.)

source.place: Limits, Proposition 05YU (label proposition-affine, limits.tex line 2875), with its proof (S separated by Morphisms lemma-image-universally-closed-separated (09MQ), f affine by Morphisms lemma-affine-permanence, f integral by Morphisms lemma-integral-universally-closed; S quasi-compact; X = lim X_i with X_i -> S finite by Limits lemma-integral-limit-finite-and-finite-presentation (09YZ); X_i affine for large i by Limits lemma-limit-affine (01Z6); conclusion by Limits lemma-affine (01ZT; Chevalley's theorem: target of a finite surjective morphism from an affine scheme is affine))

proof.text: ($X$ is separated.) Since $X$ is affine, its structure morphism $X\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf Z$ is a morphism between affine schemes, hence affine [pqf-def-affine-morphism], hence separated [lem-weil-pbc-affine-morphism-permanence] (3). So $X$ is a separated scheme in the sense of [def-weil-proper-morphism].

source.place: Limits, proof of Proposition 05YU (proposition-affine), first sentence (hypothesis of Morphisms 09MQ (2) that X is separated); the agent writes out why an affine scheme is separated (Morphisms 01S7)

proof.text: ($S$ is separated.) Let $p:X\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf Z$ and $q:S\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf Z$ be the structure morphisms. Since $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf Z$ is a final object (a morphism into $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf Z$ is a ring map $\mathbf Z\to\Gamma$, which is unique [lem-weil-pbc-morphism-into-affine-scheme]), $q\circ f=p$. Now $f$ is surjective and universally closed and $p$ is separated by step 1, so [lem-weil-pbc-surjective-universally-closed-separated] (Morphisms 09MQ (4) over the base $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf Z$, which is 09MQ (2)) gives that $q$ is separated, i.e. $S$ is separated.

source.place: Limits, proof of Proposition 05YU, first sentence ('By Morphisms, Lemma 09MQ the scheme S is separated'); Morphisms 09MQ proof, parts (1), (2) from (3), (4) with S = Spec Z

proof.text: ($f$ is affine, hence integral.) $X$ is affine and $S$ is separated (step 2), so $f$ is an affine morphism by [lem-weil-pbc-affine-source-separated-target-affine-morphism] (Morphisms 01SG (4)). Since $f$ is affine and universally closed, $f$ is integral by [pqf-lem-integral-univclosed] (Morphisms 01WM, (2) $\Rightarrow$ (1)).

source.place: Limits, proof of Proposition 05YU, first paragraph (Morphisms lemma-affine-permanence, then lemma-integral-universally-closed)

proof.text: ($S$ is quasi-compact and quasi-separated.) The structure morphism $X\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf Z$ is affine (step 1), hence quasi-compact and quasi-separated [lem-weil-pbc-affine-morphism-permanence] (3); as $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf Z$ is affine, $X$ is quasi-compact [lem-weil-pbc-qcqs-over-affine]. Since $f$ is surjective [def-weil-surjective-morphism], $|S|=f(|X|)$ is the image of a quasi-compact space under a continuous map, hence quasi-compact. The diagonal $S\to S\times_{\mathbf Z}S$ is a closed immersion (step 2), hence affine [lem-weil-pbc-closed-immersion-integral-separated-uc] (b), hence quasi-compact [lem-weil-pbc-affine-morphism-permanence] (3); so $S$ is quasi-separated [def-weil-pbc-scheme-conventions].

source.place: Limits, proof of Proposition 05YU, second paragraph ('Since f is surjective and X is quasi-compact we also deduce that S is quasi-compact'); quasi-separatedness of the separated S (needed for Limits 09YZ) is written out by the agent

proof.text: (Approximation by finite morphisms.) By steps 3 and 4, $f$ is integral and $S$ is quasi-compact and quasi-separated, so by [lem-weil-pbc-integral-morphism-limit-of-finite] (Limits 09YZ) there are a directed set $I$, $S$-schemes $\nu_i:X_i\to S$ that are finite (and of finite presentation) [def-weil-finite-integral-morphism], affine transition morphisms $X_{i'}\to X_i$ over $S$ for $i'\ge i$, and morphisms $p_i:X\to X_i$ over $S$ (so $f=\nu_i\circ p_i$) making $X=\varprojlim_iX_i$ in the category of schemes.

source.place: Limits, proof of Proposition 05YU, third paragraph, first sentence (Lemma 09YZ, lemma-integral-limit-finite-and-finite-presentation)

proof.text: (Some $X_i$ is affine.) Each $\nu_i$ is finite, hence affine [def-weil-finite-integral-morphism], hence quasi-compact and quasi-separated [lem-weil-pbc-affine-morphism-permanence] (3); since $S$ is quasi-compact and quasi-separated (step 4), every $X_i$ is quasi-compact and quasi-separated [lem-weil-pbc-qcqs-morphism-permanence] (2). So $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is a directed inverse system of quasi-compact quasi-separated schemes with affine transition morphisms whose limit $X$ is affine; by [lem-weil-pbc-limit-affine-stage] (Limits 01Z6) there is $i_0\in I$ with $X_{i_0}$ affine.

source.place: Limits, proof of Proposition 05YU, third paragraph, second sentence (Lemma 01Z6, lemma-limit-affine, in Situation 086P, whose hypotheses (X_i qcqs, affine transitions) the agent checks)

source.place: Limits, proof of Proposition 05YU, third paragraph ('since X -> S factors through each X_i we see that X_i -> S is surjective')

proof.text: (Conclusion.) $\nu_{i_0}:X_{i_0}\to S$ is finite (step 5) and surjective (step 7) with $X_{i_0}$ affine (step 6), so $S$ is affine by [lem-weil-pbc-finite-surjective-affine-target] (Limits 01ZT, Chevalley's theorem). For the parenthetical remark: an integral morphism is affine and universally closed [pqf-lem-integral-univclosed] (Morphisms 01WM, (1) $\Rightarrow$ (2)), so the statement applies to a surjective integral $f$.
